speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: My response will also address written Parliamentary Questions raised by Dr Hamid Razak in today's Order Paper, and a similar question raised by Ms Mariam Jaafar scheduled for a subsequent Sitting.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: If the Members are satisfied with the response, they may wish to withdraw their questions after this session.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Over the past few years, patient load has been shifting from private hospitals to public hospitals.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The issue of insurance and insurance riders is not the reason why patient load is shifting from private to public.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: This has been happening for the last 15 years and there are many reasons.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Part of it is that as people get older, some of them prefer public hospitals, where there are more disciplines and more holistic care.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Another key reason is the escalating cost of private healthcare.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: That is in turn fuelled by Integrated Shield Plan (IP) riders, which provide overly generous health insurance coverage, and that leads to a greater tendency for over-servicing and over-consumption of healthcare services.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Higher private healthcare cost is translated into higher private hospital IP rider premiums.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And I suspect amongst them, many switched from using private to public hospitals.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: To Dr Hamid’s question on the indicators that we used as a basis to decide policies, the data and signs have been clear and the situation is not ideal and not sustainable.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We have been actively expanding healthcare infrastructure and expanding manpower in order to cope with rising workload and manage wait times.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Our plans are significant, I have made them public before and I will not repeat here.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: To Mr Yip’s question, the new requirements for IP riders will only affect policyholders who purchased riders on or after 27 November 2025.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Individual IP insurers will decide on their approach for rider policyholders who purchased their plans before 27 November 2025.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: As for affected IP riders, and these are the new ones, we should expect the following changes.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Second, the new IP rider policies will not cover the minimum IP deductibles and also require higher co-payment.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We share Members’ concerns about patients’ out-of-pocket costs, especially for large medical bills.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But this is precisely the main aim of the rider changes: preserve the protection against very large, unexpected medical bills, but disallow coverage of the minimum deductible, which is a fixed sum, which users of private hospitals tend to be able to afford.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: This would help restore health insurance to its original objective, which is to provide assurance against large, infrequent, often unexpected healthcare bills, rather than the small bills.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: For a rider plan designed with the new requirements, there will still be a cap of 5% co-payment up to $6,000 a year, in addition to the deductibles.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: In reality, these need not be out-of-pocket cash payments because patients can tap on their MediSave.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We project that six in 10 rider claimants should not have to pay cash out-of-pocket after MediSave.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: For the remaining four in 10, majority of those with cash out-of-pocket would pay $1,000 or less, and practically all will pay $3,000 or less.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We should bear in mind that most of the affected claimants that I am talking about pertain to private hospital patients.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Their IP rider premiums have been driven up so high that under the new design, many can expect significant premium savings which can more or less offset the higher co-payments.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: In short, the current design of IP riders may no longer make financial sense for many policyholders and this change will help redress the situation.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: A 60-year-old on a private hospital IP and rider with maximum coverage, can now save about $1,600 a year in premiums by switching to the new rider.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Over three years, he would have saved $4,800 in cash, which would be more than sufficient to offset the increase in co-payment for a typical procedure – for instance, $3,300 for a knee joint replacement surgery in a private hospital.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Ms Poh asked about support measures for families facing unaffordable out-of-pocket expenses.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Patients should consider their financial and healthcare needs when choosing where to seek care, including seeking subsidised care in public hospitals should affordability become an issue.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Third impact, there should be, in the medium to long term, changes in the respective utilisation of private and public care and wait times.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: As I explained earlier, this change is part of our efforts to mitigate the shift of patients from private to public healthcare that has happened over the last 10 to 15 years, by putting the private healthcare sector and health insurance on a more sustainable path and ensuring private care remains accessible to Singaporeans in the long term.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: However, in the short term, as a few Members have expressed concern about, some individuals on the new riders may choose to seek care at public hospitals to reduce their co-payment.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Efforts to expand public health capacity – both in terms of hospital beds and outpatient capacity – are already ongoing to support the demands of an ageing population.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: If need be, we may need to implement surge capacity for selected treatments.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: MOH’s key role is to oversee the development and operation of the public healthcare system and ensure universal access to healthcare.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: For individuals who prefer private healthcare and purchase private insurance, we should not micro-manage or prescribe the market practices.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: MOH has been and will continue working with key stakeholders including insurers, healthcare providers, hospitals, medical professionals and consumer representatives through the Multilateral Healthcare Insurance Committee on these matters, to strike a balance between the interests of all stakeholders.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: To sum up, we must take a long-term and balanced view of this issue so that we can put private healthcare and insurance on a more sustainable path.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Minister, I filed this Parliamentary Question (PQ) because I have received much feedback from many seniors in my constituency who have concerns about the new rider requirements.
I understand that policyholders may keep existing riders, but insurers may respond by re-pricing or adjusting the benefits that amount to the de facto coverage reduction.
What specific safeguards will MOH impose to prevent such indirect erosion of benefits, especially for ageing policyholders with limited options?

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The most important safeguard is to make sure that IP rider policies are sustainable.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, while at the point of being sold the policies, the agent probably told them, "Buy all these for peace of mind – not just peace of mind, but absolute peace of mind, you do not have to worry".

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But that went down a path of unsustainability.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, while you enjoy it for a while, it is obvious, through my answer, that I have explained, it is becoming unsustainable.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Because when there is over-coverage, in a private hospital, the bill just goes up.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: You cannot blame anybody; it is just the way human nature is.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Somebody else is paying for most of the bill, so between doctor and patient, somehow, you will oversupply and I will overconsume.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And the bill just keeps on going up at an unsustainable pace.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And it still comes back to the consumer, to the patient, in terms of higher premiums – which is why, now, the same residents that gave the Member the feedback, is also screaming, "Why is my IP rider premium going up at 20% a year?" It is because cost is going up.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We need to tackle the issue at the root and our strong hypothesis is – in fact, there is a lot of literature on this – over-coverage just leads to wastage and cost increases.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, explain to your residents: choose this new rider; tell them they are paying very high premiums, rising premiums now for a tail risk, and it may not be worth it.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Do their calculations, talk to their financial advisors.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: For someone in their 70s, that is a lot.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Someone in their 60s saves about $2,000 a year.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: That money saved – it differs from case to case – often is more than enough to pay the deductibles and co-payment.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: How would MOH prevent adverse selection, that is, those who have existing riders continue to over-consume medical services; or those who actually do not have the means to finance the co-payments and deductibles, then, decide to give up their existing riders and may, possibly, end up delaying their treatment?

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: There are a few questions in that question, I think.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: You can always come back to public healthcare.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And we are expanding the system; we are recruiting manpower.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: While we are very busy, this is our commitment to all Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, on the healthcare front, be assured that it is always universal healthcare through the public health system.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: As for others, who continue to stay on their riders, I think they are also feeling the pinch.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: As I mentioned to Mr Yip just now, IP rider premiums are going up at a very fast rate because cost is going up at a very fast rate.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Because there is over-generous coverage, leading to overconsumption, unnecessary treatment.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, many existing rider policyholders are also rethinking.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Increasingly, over dinner tables, amongst friends and colleagues, more people are thinking about their rider policies, that they may not be worth it.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: With these changes, with this signalling, I think more may do so.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: At some point, insurance companies have to do their calculations.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Year to year, they do change their terms and conditions, and we have to see what they intend to do with existing rider policyholders.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: The reason I asked the PQ is that there has been lots of sentiments from my colleagues in the restructured hospitals that waiting times for subsidised patients have been increasing.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: They are worried that with this new rider that is coming up from April that those who are on private riders will then switch to public healthcare because of the higher cost-sharing that is in place.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Will the Ministry and the Minister be able to reassure that there is data in place to say that this new rider principles will, in fact, continue to encourage those with private riders to remain in private healthcare?

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: And also reassure that insurance companies will not make unilateral decisions on premium hikes, for example, which, again, will deter our residents from staying in the private healthcare and this will give rise to a surge capacity in our public institutions as well?

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And when insurance companies find that cost is going up and they are barely making – most of them are actually making losses on their private hospital insurance portfolio – they will end up raising premiums.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: This is something we are watching, but this is a commercial arrangement, something that they may do.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I am equally concerned as them, which is why we are making this move.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Because, as I mentioned earlier, over 10, 15 years, the shift is very discernible, away from private into public and as I mentioned, a key reason is the rising cost in private hospitals.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It is because IP riders are fuelling that cost increase, shifting people from private to public.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It makes a lot more sense when someone who has the ability to buy private healthcare insurance, including a rider, wants to use private insurance.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But half of them, today, switch to public subsidised care, for whatever reasons.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It will help the entire system and in particular, the public healthcare system, if more of them who can afford it, stay with private hospital care.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And so, private hospital care has to become more accessible, more affordable.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But we cannot do that without this adjustment in IP rider policy.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, please tell your colleagues that my and my colleagues in MOH's assurance is that we are watching this closely.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Wait times are very important to us, capacity adequacy is very important to us and their well-being is very important to us.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: MOH itself notes a trend of escalating cost and premiums alongside tightening claims practices.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: MAS can act on unfair claims handling, but MAS is primarily a financial regulator.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: MOH's direct levers seem strongest when policies are MediSave-linked.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: So, my question is, what enforceable levers does MOH have to ensure that insurer conduct advances healthcare affordability and access?

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: And where does MOH remain dependent on MAS?

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Also, it appears to me that no one is cleanly accountable for insurer behaviour as a health system actor.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Does the Minister believe that this is a gap that requires filling?

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And I think that shows accountability that when something is not sustainable, not working in the best interest of the patients and people, we will take action.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And I think we have more than enough levers to do so.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: There is a part of Mr Tiong's question that talks about panel doctors.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: What we want to make sure is that Government's main responsibility is actually to run the public healthcare system to ensure universal accessibility.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But when it comes to private healthcare, we let the market operate.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But if the market cannot operate in a laissez-faire manner, we will regulate.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But we should not be tempted to become micro-managing, because it is the worst thing to do to say that we leave it to the market, but we micro-manage all their actions and behaviour.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I think that is the worst of both worlds.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But we already have a huge nationalised system in public healthcare.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, for private healthcare, control the important levers, control the key parameters, but let the market operate.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Is there sufficient surge capacity in our healthcare system to deal with more private patients coming in after this policy change, especially for smaller procedures that are under the deductible limit?

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Again, I will want to remind the Member that because of the ageing population, demand has been going up.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: There has also been a trend, a secular trend of private hospital patients moving to public.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, whatever problem that the Member is painting now, it has been happening for the last 15, 20 years.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And it is an issue we are most concerned about.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We have spoken in this Chamber, many times how we are expanding capacity, ensuring people are healthy, moderating the demand by controlling chronic diseases.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But IP riders are an additional fuel to the fire that we are facing, which is, mainly, an ageing population pushing up healthcare demand.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, we will continue to expand the system and take a multi-prong approach to both increase supply and moderating the demand for healthcare, especially unnecessary treatment and wastage.
